titre: Authenticating an object no one saw come out of the ground
accroche: Looted in 1999, sold on the black market, recovered by the police in a Basel hotel: the origin of the Nebra disk had to be reconstructed after the fact
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 4, 1999, two men equipped with metal detectors dug without permission at the summit of the Mittelberg, a hill near Nebra, Germany. One of them uncovered with a pickax a bronze disk overlaid with gold, decorated with a celestial body, a crescent, and thirty-two stars, and damaged it in the process. The pair sold the whole find to a fence for 32,000 marks. The object changed hands again, ending up with a private collector who acquired it for 236,000 marks.

In February 2002, the regional archaeologist Harald Meller organized a sting operation with the police. On February 23, in a hotel in Basel, he posed as a buyer while the sellers demanded 700,000 marks. Once the pieces had been examined, the police arrested the two fences. The disk joined the Landesmuseum in Halle.

## Authenticating without having excavated

An object removed from the ground with no archaeologist present poses a problem that science has to solve after the fact: how do you know it is authentic, and where it really comes from?

Meller's team reopened the Mittelberg. There they found traces of bronze and soil whose composition matched that still stuck to the disk and to the objects found with it: two swords, two axes, a chisel, two arm spirals. The patina on the bronze, for its part, cannot be faked in a few years; its analysis confirms an ancient burial. Radiocarbon applied to the birch bark that wrapped the sword hilts dates it to the 16th or 15th century BCE. A chemical analysis even traces the provenance of the metals: the gold is thought to come from Cornwall, the copper from the Austrian Mitterberg.

In 2020, two German researchers challenged this dating and proposed attributing the disk to the Iron Age, several centuries later. A team of thirteen authors, including Meller and the geochemist Ernst Pernicka, answered them in the journal Archaeologia Austriaca by assembling all the available interdisciplinary evidence. The debate is not closed in its details, but the Early Bronze Age dating remains the best supported by the combined data.

## An object that had already changed several times

What the investigation also revealed is that the disk on display today is not the one that was first made. Two gold arcs, added later along its edges, cover two of the original stars; a third star was moved so it would stay visible. Another arc, with striated edges, was then inserted between the stars. Then the disk was pierced, probably so it could be carried or hung in a different way. Finally, one of the two edge arcs was removed, before the final burial around 1600 BCE.

The disk that a court ended up having authenticated is therefore not a snapshot. It is an object reworked, corrected, and reinterpreted by its successive owners, perhaps over several generations, before being hidden underground, then stolen, then found again.

repere.texte: In the hilts of the swords found with the disk, remains of birch bark were radiocarbon-dated to the 16th or 15th century BCE.

carte.punch: A looted object, sold on the black market, recovered in a Basel hotel
carte.idee: In 1999, two looters dig up a bronze disk with gold stars in Germany. Secretly resold for three years, it is recovered by the police in Basel in 2002. With no proper excavation, its authenticity had to be reconstructed after the fact, from the soil, the patina, and radiocarbon.

quiz.question: Why did so many different analyses have to be carried out to authenticate the Nebra disk?
choix: Because bronze is an alloy impossible to tell apart from a modern copy
Because the looters had repainted the disk before reselling it
Because no German laboratory was equipped to do radiocarbon dating
Because it was found outside any controlled archaeological excavation context
quiz.explication: The disk was extracted clandestinely, with no archaeologist present: what a proper excavation would have established on site therefore had to be reconstructed after the fact, through the soil, the patina, radiocarbon, and the chemistry of the metals. Bronze can indeed be dated through its context, and no repainting is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what material was radiocarbon dating performed?
choix: On the gold of the stars fixed to the disk's surface
On the birch bark wrapped around the sword hilts
On the soil still stuck to the back of the bronze disk
On the bronze of the disk itself, sampled at the edge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Radiocarbon dates only organic matter: neither gold nor bronze lends itself to it. What was dated was the remains of birch bark found in the hilts of the swords buried with the disk, to the 16th or 15th century BCE.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where do the disk's metals come from, according to chemical analysis?
choix: Gold from Cornwall, copper from the Austrian Mitterberg
Gold and copper both from mines near Nebra
Gold from the Black Sea, copper from the French Alps
Gold from Bohemia, copper from the German Harz massif
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The chemistry of metals makes it possible to trace them back to their original deposit: the gold has been traced to Cornwall and the copper to the Mitterberg, in Austria. This is one of the cross-checked lines of evidence supporting the Bronze Age dating.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the examination reveal about the history of the disk itself?
choix: It was made in one piece, then buried right away
It was assembled from two older disks
It was modified several times, with arcs covering stars
It was re-engraved by the looters before the 1999 resale
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Two gold arcs added along the edges cover two original stars, a third star was moved so it would stay visible, another arc was inserted afterward, then the disk was pierced and one of the arcs removed. The object on display is not the one that was first made.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the disk recovered in February 2002?
choix: By a seizure carried out at the private collector's home
By the looters voluntarily handing it back to the police
By a court canceling an auction sale
By a sting operation in a Basel hotel
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The regional archaeologist Harald Meller posed as a buyer on February 23, 2002, while the sellers demanded 700,000 marks. The police stepped in once the pieces had been examined, and the disk joined the Landesmuseum in Halle.
